title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarks & Runbooks
author: Ava Patel
content:
Overview:

This document consolidates the serving runtime reference material used by the eng-serving-runtime team: runtime architecture, kernel scheduling policy and implementation notes, profiling and regression playbooks, the canonical benchmarking suite and baselines, release notes for recent runtime releases, known issues, operational runbooks, and pointers to the team wiki and lower-level pages. The target audience is runtime engineers, SREs, performance engineers, and platform owners.

Goals and scope:
- Describe the production serving runtime components and responsibilities.
- Capture kernel scheduling design and configuration used in production.
- Provide a repeatable profiling and regression triage playbook.
- Document the benchmarking suite, standard workloads, and baselines.
- Provide runbooks for common operational incidents (latency tail, OOMs, kernel thrash).
- Maintain a single reference for recent release notes and known issues.

Ownership & contacts:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-infra subteam)
- Oncall: runtime-sre rotation (pager: #runtime-oncall)
- Slack channels: #runtime-engineering, #runtime-perf, #runtime-incidents
- Pager duty escalation: See team wiki -> oncall escalation matrix

High-level runtime architecture (summary):
- Dispatcher (api-gateway compatible): accepts user requests and enforces auth, quotas, and routing policies.
- Router: policy engine that selects host pool / model variant based on latency/cost/region/tenant.
- Batcher: accumulates requests and forms micro-batches based on model, sequence-length bucket, and latency SLO.
- Scheduler (kernel scheduler): assigns work to GPU lanes and selects kernels, handles preemption/backpressure.
- Runtime workers: per-GPU process (or container) managing model loading, KV cache, token generation loop, and device memory.
- Kernel selector & kernel cache: maps model op patterns to optimized kernels (cuBLAS/cutlass/custom CUDA kernels, Triton kernels, and CPU fallbacks).
- KV cache & prefix cache layer: prefix caching + sharding across GPUs for conversational workloads.
- Telemetry & tracing: traces per-request latency, token generation timelines, kernel-level metrics (via nsys/metrics-exporters).

Architecture diagram (text):
API -> Dispatcher -> Router -> Batcher -> Scheduler -> [GPU Worker (kernel selector + exec loop + KV cache)] -> Telemetry/Tracing

Design principles for kernel scheduling:
- Minimize tail latency while maintaining high throughput and device utilization.
- Prefer affinity-based placement: colocate requests with warm KV-caches and pinned model shards.
- Avoid long-running blocking kernels on latency-sensitive lanes (canary lanes).
- Use adaptive batching with per-model and per-tenant latency targets.
- Support graceful preemption: short-running low-priority tasks can be preempted in favor of high-priority (SLO-critical) traffic.

Key scheduling primitives and terms:
- Lane: a logical GPU execution queue (e.g., latency-lane, batch-lane, background-lane).
- Slot: reservation unit in a lane (counts tokens or micro-batch).
- Affinity key: (tenant_id, model_id, kv_shard) used by scheduler to prefer placement.
- KernelPolicy: a runtime table that maps (model-op, sequence-length, hardware) -> kernel variant + heuristic (eager vs streaming).

Kernel scheduling policy (summary):
1) Admission: incoming batcher candidates are classified by priority (latency-critical vs best-effort).
2) Affinity placement: try to place on workers with warm KV cache and matching kernel profiles.
3) Lane selection: prefer latency-lanes for p50/p95-critical requests, batch-lanes for throughput requests.
4) Kernel selection: pick kernel variant by KernelPolicy; prefer quantized faster kernels if quality profile passes.
5) Preemption rules: if latency-lane is free but occupied by a best-effort job older than X ms, preempt older job (checkpoint state) and schedule latency job.

Example scheduler configuration (production values):
--- yaml snippet ---
scheduler:
  lanes:
    - name: latency
      priority: 100
      max_concurrent_slots: 24
      preemptible: false
    - name: batch
      priority: 50
      max_concurrent_slots: 128
      preemptible: true
  affinity_cache_ttl_ms: 300000  # 5 minutes
  preemption_threshold_ms: 250
  kernel_policy_reload_interval_s: 60
--- end snippet ---

Notes on kernel choices:
- For short sequences (< 128 tokens) prefer fused attention kernels; for long sequences prefer tiled kernels with KV streaming.
- Quantized int8 kernels used for 70% of production requests on T4/A10g where model quality evaluators passed.
- CPU fallback kernels used for low-cost playground instances with explicit routing policy.

Profiling and regression playbook (step-by-step):
1) Detect: alert triggers (see 'Operational alerting' section) notify team about regression (increased p95/p99 latency, error rate, or throughput drop).
2) Narrow: identify impacted model(s), hostpool, and time window via traces (jaeger/opentelemetry) and metrics (prometheus).
3) Capture: run a deterministic reproduction using the tracing-id or by replaying representative request set. Use the benchmark harness to generate the workload.
4) Collect low-level traces and counters:
   - nsys (CUDA): nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=profile_report.nsys-rep <runtime workload>
   - nvtop / nvidia-smi dmon for GPU utilization and mem usage
   - pprof (CPU): go tool pprof -http=:8080 <binary> cpu.prof
   - runtime trace: curl http://<worker>/internal/trace?trace_id=<trace_id>
5) Analyze hotspots: look for long blocking kernels (> preemption_threshold_ms), long memcpy, frequent kernel switching, or memory thrash.
6) Apply mitigations: adjust batching window, pin workload to a different lane, increase KV cache TTL, or switch kernel variant.
7) Validate: re-run the reproduction and compare latency/throughput.
8) Postmortem: create an incident review if SLOs were violated. Attach traces, profiles, and recommendation.

Profiling checklist (quick):
- Have sample request(s) that show regression (with trace IDs).
- Collect nsys and pprof traces.
- Attach Prometheus metrics: per-lane concurrency, GPU utilization, avg kernel time, memcpy time, memory allocation patterns.
- Check kernel-policy version and kernel blobs (hash) used in the run.
- Verify model shard placement and KV cache hit rate.

Benchmarking suite (canonical):
- Purpose: produce stable, repeatable performance numbers for: latency SLOs, throughput at target quality, and regression detection.
- Harness: benchmark-runner (Go) + dataset packs per model family (gpt-like, opt-like, small-decoder).
- Workloads:
  - latency-standalone: single connection steady requests designed to measure p50/p95/p99 with cold/warm KV states.
  - throughput-sustained: multi-client sustained QPS ramp to determine stable throughput at p95 <= configured target.
  - mixed-traffic: realistic mix of short prompts + chat history to measure mixed-case performance.
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 latency (request & token), throughput (tokens/sec), GPU utilization, memory high-water mark, KV cache hit rate, model quality regression (BLEU/perplexity where applicable).

Standard benchmark run command (example):
$ ./benchmark-runner --model gpt-redwood-3b --profile latency-standalone --clients 4 --duration 300 --trace-output traces/2028-01-12

Canonical baseline (example numbers on A100-80GB for gpt-redwood-3b, warm KV):
| metric | value |
|-------|-------|
| p50 request latency | 28ms |
| p95 request latency | 84ms |
| p99 request latency | 150ms |
| tokens/sec (sustained, multi-client) | 18000 |
| GPU util (tokens kernels) | 82% |
(Note: baselines are representative; always run the benchmark harness for precise numbers on specific hardware.)

Release notes (recent major runtime release):
- Version: runtime-2.9.0 (deployed 2027-11-29)
  - Kernel scheduler: added lane-based preemption and affinity cache to reduce tail latency for conversational workloads.
  - Kernel selector: introduced tiled attention kernel variant for sequences > 1024 improving p99 by ~22% on A100.
  - Batcher: adaptive-batching enabled by default for dedicated pools; default batching window reduced from 12ms -> 8ms.
  - Observability: added per-kernel histograms and integrated nsys trace export endpoint.
  - Migration notes: rolling deploy requires kernel-policy and kernel-blobs be staged in S3 prior to traffic cutover. See rollout steps below.

Rollout steps (minor/major):
1) Stage new kernel blobs in S3 and mark kernel-policy in the config-store (canary tag).
2) Deploy to canary pool (latency-lane) with 5% traffic for 2 hours. Run smoke benchmarks and sanity tests.
3) If no regressions, increase to 25% for 4 hours and run full benchmark-suite.
4) Full rollout by percentage based on pool healthboards and error budgets.

Known issues (production):
- ISSUE-2028-01: Kernel selector thrash on mixed sequence-length workloads
  - Symptom: frequent kernel-switching, increased context-switch overhead, elevated p99.
  - Workaround: pin workload to sequence-length bucket via router; increase affinity_cache_ttl to reduce re-placement.
  - Status: in_progress (kernel-policy heuristics under revision).
- ISSUE-2027-12: Intermittent OOM on background-lane during large-batch model updates
  - Symptom: worker OOM when multiple model rollout downloads coincide with background infer jobs.
  - Workaround: throttle background-lane concurrent downloads and increase model-pull backoff jitter.
  - Status: mitigated (config change rolled out 2027-12-06).
- ISSUE-2027-09: Profiling artifacts missing for some nsys captures on older CUDA drivers
  - Symptom: incomplete nsys output files; missing API traces.
  - Workaround: upgrade driver to minimum supported version 525.x or use CPU-side tracing until upgrade.
  - Status: known; scheduled in infra-driver upgrade Jan 2028.

Operational runbooks (concise):
1) High p99 latency (tail regression):
   a) Confirm alert: Check p99 latency metric and associated error budget.
   b) Query traces to find affected model/pool.
   c) If kernel-switch thrash detected, temporarily route traffic to an unthrashed pool or use model-variant with stable kernel-policy.
   d) If KV cache miss spikes, increase cache TTL for the affected model and pin to workers with warm caches.
   e) If no quick mitigation, engage runtime oncall and open incident with trace ids and nsys captures.
2) GPU OOMs on a worker:
   a) Verify logs and OOM reason.
   b) Evict low-priority batch-lane slots using the scheduler admin API: POST /admin/scheduler/evict?lane=batch&count=10
   c) Restart worker with safe-mode (disable background downloads): /usr/local/bin/runtime --safe-mode
   d) Investigate model sizes and shard placement; consider reducing max_concurrent_slots for batch lane.
3) Kernel scheduler thrash (frequent context switching):
   a) Identify frequent kernel changes in traces.
   b) Increase affinity_cache_ttl and disable kernel-policy auto-reload temporarily.
   c) Roll back to previous kernel-policy hash if recent policy change correlated with regression.

Operational alerts (examples & thresholds):
- runtime.p99_request_latency > 200ms for 5m -> P1
- runtime.error_rate > 0.5% for 10m -> P1
- gpu.mem.high_wm > 95% -> P2
- kernel.preemption_rate > 20% for 10m -> P2

Appendix: SLOs and common config keys
- SLOs:
  - p50 request latency (warm KV): <= 40ms
  - p95 request latency (warm KV): <= 120ms
  - p99 request latency (warm KV): <= 200ms
  - tokens/sec per A100 GPU (mixed): target 16k-22k depending on model family
- Common config keys (admin/config-store):
  - scheduler.lanes.*.max_concurrent_slots
  - scheduler.affinity_cache_ttl_ms
  - kernel_policy.version
  - kernel_blobs.s3_path
  - batcher.window_ms

Maintenance checklist for new kernel-policy rollout:
1) Stage kernel blobs in s3 and update kernel_policy.version (canary tag).
2) Run smoke benchmark on canary pool.
3) Check telemetry: kernel histograms, preemption_rate, p99 latency.
4) If OK, promote kernel_policy.version to prod and start ramp.
5) Monitor for at least 24h at 100% before deprecating old blobs.
